title: Quaternion Message Passing Neural Network (QMPNN) construction

organized_parts.label: other
organized_parts.content: A general construction that maps any real-valued message-passing GNN layer into a quaternion-valued layer

organized_parts.label: elaboration
organized_parts.content: is specified by (i) grouping every node feature vector $h_v^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^F$ into $F/4$ quaternions $h_v^{(l),Q}=h_r^{(l)}+h_i^{(l)}\mathrm{i}+h_j^{(l)}\mathrm{j}+h_k^{(l)}\mathrm{k}$ (requiring $F$ divisible by $4$), (ii) representing the layer parameters as a quaternion weight matrix $W^{(l),Q}=W_r^{(l)}+W_i^{(l)}\mathrm{i}+W_j^{(l)}\mathrm{j}+W_k^{(l)}\mathrm{k}$ where $W_r^{(l)},W_i^{(l)},W_j^{(l)},W_k^{(l)}$ are real-valued component matrices, and (iii) performing feature transforms using the Hamilton product $W^{(l),Q}\otimes h_v^{(l),Q}$ so that the transformed components are computed by the block matrix formula $$ \begin{bmatrix} \mathcal{R}(W^{(l),Q}\otimes h_v^{(l),Q})\\[6pt] \mathcal{I}(W^{(l),Q}\otimes h_v^{(l),Q})\\[6pt] \mathcal{J}(W^{(l),Q}\otimes h_v^{(l),Q})\\[6pt] \mathcal{K}(W^{(l),Q}\otimes h_v^{(l),Q}) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} W_{r}^{(l)} & -W_{i}^{(l)} & -W_{j}^{(l)} & -W_{k}^{(l)}\\[3pt] W_{i}^{(l)} & W_{r}^{(l)} & -W_{k}^{(l)} & W_{j}^{(l)}\\[3pt] W_{j}^{(l)} & W_{k}^{(l)} & W_{r}^{(l)} & -W_{i}^{(l)}\\[3pt] W_{k}^{(l)} & -W_{j}^{(l)} & W_{i}^{(l)} & W_{r}^{(l)} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} h_{r}^{(l)}\\[3pt] h_{i}^{(l)}\\[3pt] h_{j}^{(l)}\\[3pt] h_{k}^{(l)} \end{bmatrix}, $$ where $\mathcal{R},\mathcal{I},\mathcal{J},\mathcal{K}$ denote the resulting real and three imaginary component vectors.

title: Parameter-count reduction by quaternion parameterization with preserved time complexity
content: Representing layer weights as quaternion matrices and grouping four real feature channels into one quaternion reduces the number of independent trainable real parameters by a factor of four relative to an equivalent real-valued GNN weight matrix: a quaternion weight mapping from $F$ real input features to $F'$ real outputs uses $F/4\times F'/4$ quaternion entries (each with four components shared by the Hamilton product), yielding one-fourth the degrees of freedom of the corresponding real weight matrix. At the same time, quaternion matrix multiplications implemented via the Hamilton-product block structure have the same asymptotic time complexity as the corresponding real matrix multiplications, so the parameter reduction is achieved without increasing matrix-multiplication time complexity.

title: Empirical parity or improvement of QMPNNs vs real GNNs across node, link, and graph tasks
content: When QMPNN variants of standard GNN architectures (QGCN, QGAT, QSAGE) are trained under the same hyperparameters and evaluated on standard datasets, the quaternion models achieve comparable or better accuracy, ROC-AUC, or Hits@K (proportion of top-K predictions that are correct) while using roughly one-fourth of the trainable parameters. For example: (a) node classification on Cora: real GCN 85.2 ± 1.3 accuracy with 140.5K parameters vs QGCN 84.1 ± 1.5 accuracy with 42.1K parameters; (b) node classification on PubMed: GCN 79.1 ± 1.2 with 131.9K parameters vs QGCN 78.4 ± 1.4 with 41.7K parameters; (c) link prediction on CORA: GCN ROC-AUC 79.27 ± 0.47 with 96.0K parameters vs QGCN ROC-AUC 83.55 ± 0.03 with 27.2K parameters; (d) graph classification on MUTAG: GCN 83.54 ± 0.40 accuracy with 4.8K parameters vs QGCN 88.61 ± 0.66 accuracy with 4.4K parameters. Across all tasks and datasets evaluated, quaternion variants frequently perform within a small margin of the corresponding real models and sometimes exceed their performance while consistently having approximately one-fourth the trainable parameter count.

title: Graph-lottery-ticket formulation and pruning algorithms for GNNs and QMPNNs
content: A graph-lottery-ticket definition and an algorithmic procedure specialized to GNNs and QMPNNs are provided: (i) a sparsification subroutine that alternately updates model weights W and a continuous mask m via gradient steps (updating W by $W^{(i+1)} = W^{(i)} - \eta \nabla_W \mathcal{L}_{\text{task}}$ and updating m by $m^{i+1} = m^i - \lambda \nabla_{m^i} \mathcal{L}_{\text{task}}$), and finally thresholds the lowest-magnitude 20% entries of m to obtain a binary mask; and (ii) an iterative prune-rewind loop that applies the sparsification repeatedly while resetting weights to the original initialization $W^0$ to discover a binary mask m such that the masked subnetwork $f((\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E},\mathbf{X}), m \odot W^0)$ is the proposed winning graph lottery ticket. This formulation explicitly avoids pruning the input graph and instead searches for sparse parameter masks, making the resulting tickets applicable to graph-level tasks and transfer learning.

title: Existence of graph lottery tickets (GLTs) in QMPNNs at high sparsity
content: Winning graph-lottery tickets exist for both real-valued GNNs and QMPNNs: magnitude-based iterative pruning identifies subnetworks that match baseline performance at sparsity levels down to approximately 1–20% of the original parameter count (i.e., retaining 1–20% of weights) across multiple architectures (QGCN, QGAT, QSAGE) and tasks.

title: QMPNNs scale to large graphs while preserving performance
content: QMPNN variants scale to large graph datasets and maintain performance comparable to real-valued GNNs while using fewer parameters: on OGBN-Arxiv node classification, GCN achieves 72.8 ± 1.5 accuracy with 145.1K parameters versus QGCN 72.3 ± 1.6 with 43.5K parameters; on OGBG-COLLAB link prediction, QGCN achieves Hits@50 45.80 ± 1.35 with 6.4K parameters compared to GCN 44.02 ± 1.57 with 12.5K parameters. Thus the quaternion reparameterization is effective on large-scale graph benchmarks.
